QuestionAnswer
Q3: how are price, trade size and wallet volume distributed?Descriptive, no pre-registered criterion. Median trade size 6.93 USDC, mean 129.8 USDC. Trade size fits, KS D: normal 0.4686 and exponential 0.5343 (both fitted on all data), power law 0.03883 (fitted on the top 10% tail only). The fits are not ranked. Lognormal was not compared. Mean price p_1d 0.3757.
Q1: do prices match how often events happen?Prices are not calibrated as a whole at this n. chi-square 67.99 (df 10), p < 0.0001, largest per-bin gap -0.0329 (bin 7), n 47,948. bins off bh 5, bins off bonferroni 4, mean squared residual of the price 0.1071.
Q2: who is the crowd? Do a few wallets do most of the trading?Yes by USDC volume, far beyond the 80/20 reference. The top 20% of wallets hold 98.9% of maker volume and 98.0% of taker volume, against 80% for the 80/20 rule. Volume is the USDC sum over every trade in the 47,948 kept markets, including trades after T - 1 day. Trade counts were not measured. The 80/20 rule and the power law come from Lecture 6. For the top 10% of wallet-role rows, the fitted power-law exponent alpha is 1.788. The KS test rejects an exact power law (KS D 0.024, p < 0.0001). The redrawn CCDF tail bends downward at the largest wallets, so it is not a straight line on log-log axes. We do not say wallet volume follows a power law, and we set no line for how close. There is no pre-registered verdict for this. The top 1% of maker wallets hold 86.1% of maker volume. A wallet is an address, not a person.

Table 1. Questions and answers. Verdicts come from verdicts.json, numbers from the saved results.

How to read

  • Each answer repeats numbers from the sections below. Check the p-value together with the effect size.
  • With tens of thousands of markets, a small effect can give a tiny p. Read the effect size first.
  • Tests assume independent markets. Markets on one event are not independent.
  • The z intervals assume the same independence, so they may be too narrow.

How to read

  • D is the size of the gap between the data and one fit, p only says if the gap is zero. The power law D covers the tail only, so do not compare it with the others. Lognormal was not compared.
  • KS p-values are optimistic for fitted parameters. The fit used the same data as the test.
  • Mean far above median means a long right tail: a few large trades and wallets.
  • Wallet volume pools maker and taker rows, so one address can appear twice.
Step 4 of 7

Q1: calibration

Asks: when the price is p, does the event happen about p of the time? (price at T - 1 day, 10 equal-width bins)

Model: each market's outcome is Bernoulli(p), where p is its price. If prices are calibrated, the outcome-1 count in a bin is binomial(n, mean p). The chi-square test used here is the goodness-of-fit form of the chi-square test in Lecture 12: observed against expected counts, expected from the prices.

Table 13. Robustness: equal-frequency bins, main set. BH p and call are from run 142140_q1eqfreq_v5 (code v5), on the same markets.

In equal-frequency bins the z interval puts the price outside 8 bins, and BH marks 7. They differ in bin (0.0, 0.00122] (1 outcome-1 in 4,795). The z interval has no correction for ten bins. Its spread comes from the observed rate, which is unreliable when a bin has very few outcome-1 results.

How to read

  • Pre-registered line: chi-square p < 0.05 means prices are not calibrated as a whole.
  • A bin is off when its BH-corrected p < 0.05. A negative difference means the event happened less often than priced.
  • The effect is small, and it runs one way. In 9 of 10 bins the observed rate of outcome 1 is below the mean price, so outcome 1 is priced too high. Outcome 1 is the first-listed outcome of a market. Its label is Yes in 63.9% of the kept markets. The same holds without the minimum-trade filter (9 of 10) and in equal-frequency bins (9 of 10). Over all 47,948 markets the net gap is -0.99 percentage points, 475 fewer outcome-1 results than the prices imply. The largest per-bin gap is -0.0329, in bin 7 (price 0.7 to 0.8). The largest chi-square contributor is bin 0 (31.3% of the chi-square). We set no size line before the results, so small is our reading. The p-values assume independent markets, so they are optimistic.
  • In 5 of 10 bins the mean price is outside the z interval: bins 0, 1, 6, 7, 8. These are the same bins as the BH bins off. The z interval assumes independent markets, like the tests. Markets on one event move together, so it may be too narrow.
  • The longshot statement holds only with the minimum-trade filter. Without it, bin 0 changes sign (+0.0005, BH p 0.6006) and bin 1 is -0.0093 (BH p 0.1362). Neither passes BH.
  • Mean squared residual of the price is the mean of (price minus outcome) squared. 0.25 is a coin flip at 0.5, 0 is perfect. The pre-registration calls it the Brier score.

Asks: do a few wallets hold most of the volume, and do makers differ from takers?

Yes by USDC volume, far beyond the 80/20 reference. The top 20% of wallets hold 98.9% of maker volume and 98.0% of taker volume, against 80% for the 80/20 rule. For the top 10% of wallet-role rows, the fitted power-law exponent alpha is 1.788. The KS test rejects an exact power law (KS D 0.024, p < 0.0001). The redrawn CCDF tail bends downward at the largest wallets, so it is not a straight line on log-log axes. We do not say wallet volume follows a power law, and we set no line for how close. Step 6 of 7

Robustness v3

Descriptive only, with no verdict. The Q1 verdict in this report is unchanged. Run 150310_r3_review_fixes_v6, code v6, pre-registration analysis/prereg_review_fixes.md (commit aef0808). Gate: the kept set was rebuilt (47,948 markets) and the main chi-square matched (67.99): passed. Logistic calibration, Brier skill score and the cluster bootstrap chi-square are outside the lectures (D-039).

M1: price definition

The main price is the last trade at or before T - 1 day. Does another price definition change the net gap (outcome minus price)? Main -0.99 pp, volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of the last 24 hours -1.20 pp, trade-based midpoint -1.13 pp on the 37,446 markets with both sides. Buyer-initiated trades give -2.62 pp and seller-initiated trades give +0.34 pp. The mean half-spread proxy is 1.57 pp, and the main gap lies inside it. The side sign check is validated.

M2: markets labelled Yes/No

Markets labelled Yes/No (30,112) have net gap -1.32 pp, 95% interval [-1.61, -1.03] pp. Chi-square 100.1 (df 10), p < 0.0001, 7 of 10 bins off by Benjamini-Hochberg (BH). The other 17,836 markets have chi-square p 0.1335 and net gap -0.43 pp. In markets labelled Yes/No, Yes is priced above its observed rate. The main result keeps the label outcome 1 (D-040).

M3: cluster bootstrap with proxy keys

Markets on one event are not independent, and the event key is not in the saved tables. Two proxy keys (slug stem, topic x close hour) group the markets, and the bootstrap resamples whole groups. The each-market row has no clustering. The gap interval and the cluster chi-square are outside the lectures (D-039). The call is the same for all three rows: Prices are not calibrated as a whole at this n.

M4: kept against dropped markets

Kept markets are 47,948 of 688,131 in scope (7.0%). Dropped: Up/Down 37.1%, no price 31.3%, price too old 11.7%, no winner label 9.1%, fewer than 10 trades 3.9%. Median volume over all trades is 13,372 USDC for kept markets and 142.7 USDC for the eligible dropped markets. Outcome-1 rate is 36.6% and 35.7%. The old-price group has net gap -0.35 pp and the few-trades group -1.10 pp.

M5: practical size

Logistic calibration fit, outside the lectures (D-039): intercept -0.089, slope 1.028. The implied gap is -2.17 pp at price 0.25 and -2.22 pp at price 0.50. The practical line is the mean half-spread 1.57 pp, and 0 of 7 grid prices have an interval fully beyond it. Brier skill score, outside the lectures (D-039): 0.538 against in-sample climatology. Accuracy at 0.5 is 83.4% against 63.4% for the majority.

Step 7 of 7

Method notes and reproduce

Method notes and limits

  • KS p-values are optimistic when parameters are fitted to the same data.
  • K-means is a side analysis. The clusters describe the sample.
  • A wallet is an address, not a person.
  • Tests assume independent markets. Markets on one event are not independent.
  • Duplicate rows are kept. Volume includes trades after T - 1 day.
  • Q1 covers only markets with a trade at least 1 day before T. 215,289 markets (31.3% of scope) have none and are dropped (no_price).
  • no_outcome (62,718 markets) includes markets whose outcome_seq=1 label never traded.
  • Pre-registered verdicts exist only for scope = full runs.
